findings.quote: They are generally safe in overdose and after heart attacks (sertraline).
findings.explanation: Calling an antidepressant class 'generally safe in overdose' is a safety promise on a page read by people at raised risk of self-harm. SSRIs are less toxic than tricyclics, but citalopram and escitalopram overdose can cause QT prolongation, torsades, seizures and death (the same page says citalopram prolongs QT dose-dependently), and any SSRI overdose can cause serotonin toxicity. The post-heart-attack safety evidence is for sertraline, not the class.
findings.suggestedFix: Reword: 'Less dangerous in overdose than the older tricyclic antidepressants, although overdose (especially of citalopram or escitalopram) can still cause serious heart-rhythm effects and seizures and needs emergency care. Sertraline has the best evidence of safety after a heart attack.'

findings.quote: Angio-oedema (swelling of lips, tongue, throat) means stop for good and avoid the whole class
findings.explanation: Swelling of the lips, tongue or throat can block the airway and is an emergency, yet the class page gives no urgent-care signposting for it anywhere (classWarnings only calls it 'rare ... can occur at any time'); the ramipril medicine page says 'stop immediately and call 999'. The line is also phrased as an instruction to stop a medicine. The next bullet, cautions[2] 'Pause during vomiting, diarrhoea or dehydration to protect the kidneys', is likewise an unqualified instruction, unlike the loop-diuretic page's descriptive 'the prescriber may advise pausing'.
findings.suggestedFix: 'Angio-oedema (swelling of the lips, tongue, face or throat) is an emergency needing immediate help (999); an ACE inhibitor is not restarted afterwards and the prescriber chooses an alternative.' Reword the sick-day line descriptively: 'During vomiting, diarrhoea or dehydration the prescriber may advise pausing it temporarily.'

findings.quote: Raise levels of atorvastatin and simvastatin (not rosuvastatin or pravastatin) and the risk of myopathy; doses are limited or the statin paused.
findings.explanation: The row's 'with' field lists ciclosporin among 'Strong CYP3A4 inhibitors', then says rosuvastatin and pravastatin are not affected. Ciclosporin is not a strong CYP3A4 inhibitor (it acts mainly by inhibiting OATP1B1 and other transporters) and it raises rosuvastatin several-fold (UK SmPC: contraindicated together) and pravastatin 5-10-fold (dose capped at 20 mg); some HIV protease inhibitor combinations also raise rosuvastatin. The site's own rosuvastatin page says 'Ciclosporin: do not combine', so this class row contradicts it.
findings.suggestedFix: Delete '(not rosuvastatin or pravastatin)' and take ciclosporin out of the CYP3A4 row. If kept, give ciclosporin its own row: markedly raises most statin levels; rosuvastatin contraindicated, pravastatin dose-limited (cite BNF/SmPC).

findings.quote: or for 12-24 hours (salmeterol, formoterol, and the antimuscarinics tiotropium and ipratropium)
findings.explanation: Ipratropium is a short-acting antimuscarinic lasting about 4-6 hours, like salbutamol and terbutaline; only salmeterol and formoterol (about 12 h) and tiotropium (24 h) last 12-24 h. The sentence also sets onset ('within minutes') against duration, although formoterol also acts within minutes. A reader could take ipratropium for a once- or twice-daily maintenance bronchodilator. (The alias 'reliever inhalers' similarly covers long-acting agents that are not relievers.)
findings.suggestedFix: '... within minutes and lasting about 4-6 hours (salbutamol, terbutaline, ipratropium), or for about 12 hours (salmeterol, formoterol) to 24 hours (tiotropium)'.

findings.quote: they are taken on an empty stomach with a full glass of water, standing or sitting upright for 30 minutes
findings.explanation: The 30-minute rule (repeated in cautions[0], classWarnings[1] and classInteractions[0] 'at least 30 minutes before anything else') is the alendronate/risedronate regimen. Oral ibandronate, a listed member, needs a longer wait (UK SmPC: about 1 hour before food, drink or other medicines, and upright for 1 hour). Likewise cautions[2] 'Not with eGFR below 35' is the alendronate/zoledronic acid threshold; risedronate and ibandronate use 30. Figures from the alendronate page are presented as true of every member.
findings.suggestedFix: Say timing and kidney thresholds 'depend on the product' (or give them per member, e.g. 30 minutes for alendronate and risedronate, 60 for ibandronate); otherwise drop the figures from the class page.

findings.quote: Contraindicated in cardiogenic shock, significant aortic stenosis and, for the dihydropyridines, unstable angina.
findings.explanation: Stated class-wide but taken from the amlodipine (dihydropyridine) monograph. The contraindications that define verapamil and diltiazem (second/third-degree AV block, sick sinus syndrome, severe bradycardia, left-ventricular failure / heart failure with reduced ejection fraction) are missing, and significant aortic stenosis is a dihydropyridine contraindication rather than one of verapamil/diltiazem. It also contradicts cautions[2] on the same page, 'Severe aortic stenosis and unstable angina need specialist advice' (contraindicated vs needs advice for the same conditions).
findings.suggestedFix: Split by subgroup or soften: 'Contraindications differ by member: dihydropyridines are not used in cardiogenic shock, significant aortic stenosis or (nifedipine, felodipine) unstable angina; verapamil and diltiazem are not used in heart block, sick sinus syndrome, marked bradycardia or heart failure with reduced ejection fraction.' Make cautions[2] consistent.

findings.quote: Contraindicated in asthma with a history of bronchospasm, marked bradycardia, second- or third-degree heart block, cardiogenic shock and uncontrolled heart failure.
findings.explanation: Asthma is given three different strengths on one page: cautions[1] 'a relative contraindication', classWarnings[0] 'cardioselective agents only with specialist advice', classWarnings[1] 'Contraindicated'. The list reads like the non-selective (propranolol) monograph but cites the bisoprolol page; for cardioselective agents asthma is a reason to avoid unless there is no alternative, with specialist advice (the bisoprolol medicine page says exactly that).
findings.suggestedFix: Use one consistent statement: 'Non-selective beta blockers are contraindicated in asthma; cardioselective ones are used only when there is no alternative and under specialist advice', and cite a source that supports it.

findings.quote: Insulin is never injected when symptoms or a reading show that glucose is already low
findings.explanation: An unqualified 'never' conflicts with cautions[1] on the same page ('Never stop basal insulin in type 1 diabetes, even when not eating') and with the insulin medicine page ('never stop, even when not eating: adjust instead'). The usual advice is to treat the low first and hold or reduce mealtime (rapid-acting) insulin; basal insulin is generally still taken, with the dose adjusted on the team's advice, because omission risks ketoacidosis. As written, a person on basal-bolus treatment could omit basal insulin after a low reading.
findings.suggestedFix: Restrict it: 'Mealtime (rapid-acting) insulin is not taken until a low glucose has been treated; basal insulin is not simply omitted, and the care team gives a plan for low readings.' Or delete the line.

findings.quote: avoided where possible when breastfeeding although only very low concentrations reach breast milk
findings.explanation: UK information treats ibuprofen as a preferred painkiller while breastfeeding (only tiny amounts reach milk); the site's own ibuprofen page says so, citing NHS. A blanket 'avoided where possible' for the whole class contradicts that, and the clause undermines itself ('although only very low concentrations ...').
findings.suggestedFix: 'Ibuprofen is a preferred painkiller while breastfeeding; other NSAIDs are checked with a pharmacist or doctor first.'

findings.quote: nefopam
findings.explanation: Every class-level statement on this page is paracetamol-specific: the 'Central cyclo-oxygenase' target and targets: cox-2, 'Very few at normal doses', the 4 g/day ceiling, liver failure in overdose, N-acetylcysteine, ATC N02BE. Nefopam is pharmacologically different (centrally acting, reuptake inhibition; not a COX inhibitor) and has its own contraindications (e.g. convulsive disorders, recent myocardial infarction) and common effects (sweating, nausea, dry mouth, tachycardia, urinary retention). Listing it as a member makes the class warnings wrong for it.
findings.suggestedFix: Remove nefopam from members, or add a nefopam-specific note and confine the class-wide wording to paracetamol.

findings.quote: Thiazide-like diuretics (indapamide, bendroflumethiazide)
findings.explanation: Bendroflumethiazide is a conventional thiazide; indapamide (and chlortalidone) are the thiazide-like agents. NICE NG136 draws exactly this distinction (it prefers thiazide-like diuretics such as indapamide over conventional thiazides such as bendroflumethiazide). The same wording appears on the furosemide medicine page.
findings.suggestedFix: 'Thiazide and thiazide-like diuretics (bendroflumethiazide; indapamide)'; fix the furosemide page at the same time.

findings.quote: beta-lactam antibiotics
findings.explanation: Penicillins are one subclass of the beta-lactams, which also include cephalosporins, carbapenems and monobactams. As an alias it makes the page's class warnings (true penicillin anaphylaxis excludes the whole class; amoxicillin rash in glandular fever) read as if they applied to every beta-lactam; cross-reactivity with cephalosporins is low and assessed case by case.
findings.suggestedFix: Remove the alias, or use 'penicillin antibiotics'.

findings.quote: verapamil and diltiazem slow the heart and can cause heart block and heart failure, and are not combined with beta blockers
findings.explanation: This claim, and classInteractions[0] ('Amlodipine, diltiazem and verapamil raise simvastatin levels ...') and classInteractions[2] (verapamil/diltiazem with beta blockers), cite only 'BNF: Amlodipine' and 'BNF: Amlodipine interactions'. An amlodipine monograph cannot plausibly support statements about verapamil and diltiazem; the page's references are NHS amlodipine and NICE NG136.
findings.suggestedFix: Add the BNF verapamil and diltiazem pages (and their interaction pages) as sources for the member-specific statements, or remove those clauses until sourced.

findings.quote: andexanet alfa, which NICE recommends for life-threatening or uncontrolled bleeding on apixaban or rivaroxaban
findings.explanation: As I recall, NICE's andexanet alfa appraisal (TA697) is restricted to life-threatening or uncontrolled gastrointestinal bleeding in people on apixaban or rivaroxaban, not all such bleeding. None of the NICE references on this page is the andexanet appraisal (they are the AF guideline news item and the idarucizumab evidence summary), so the claim is not supported by the page's own references.
findings.suggestedFix: Remove 'which NICE recommends ...' (keep 'andexanet alfa for apixaban and rivaroxaban'), or add the NICE appraisal as a reference and state its actual scope.

findings.quote: Take on an empty stomach, 4 hours apart from calcium, iron, antacids and proton pump inhibitors
findings.explanation: A 4-hour gap helps with binders (calcium, iron, antacids, sucralfate, colestyramine), but PPIs reduce levothyroxine absorption by raising gastric pH, so spacing the doses does not avoid the effect; the usual response is TSH monitoring and dose review. The proton-pump-inhibitors class page lists levothyroxine as 'Altered levels or absorption; monitoring advised' (no spacing), so the two pages give different management. classInteractions[0] ('doses are separated by several hours') lumps PPIs in the same way, and the levothyroxine medicine page repeats it.
findings.suggestedFix: Take PPIs out of the 4-hour list and say instead that PPIs can lower absorption, so TSH is monitored when one is started or stopped.

findings.quote: High-intensity statins (atorvastatin 40-80 mg, rosuvastatin 20-40 mg) are used after heart attacks and strokes.
findings.explanation: These ranges follow the US ACC/AHA definition of high intensity. The cited NICE NG238 recommends atorvastatin 20 mg for primary prevention and atorvastatin 80 mg for secondary prevention, and the site's rosuvastatin page says the 40 mg dose is 'for specialist use only', so 'rosuvastatin 20-40 mg ... used after heart attacks' conflicts with it. Dose figures presented as general UK practice are not supported by the cited reference.
findings.suggestedFix: Drop the doses: 'High-intensity statin doses are used after heart attacks and strokes.'

findings.quote: also first-line for anxiety disorders, panic, OCD and PTSD
findings.explanation: In UK guidance (NICE NG116) trauma-focused psychological therapy is first-line for PTSD; an SSRI or venlafaxine is considered only if the person prefers not to have therapy or it has not helped. For generalised anxiety and panic, NICE also puts psychological treatment alongside or before drugs. 'First-line' for PTSD reflects US practice presented as general on a UK-first site.
findings.suggestedFix: 'also used for anxiety disorders, panic, OCD and (when psychological therapy is declined or has not helped) PTSD'.

findings.quote: glucagon is used for a severe hypo in someone who is unconscious or cannot take sugar by mouth
findings.explanation: Red-flag content with no urgent-care signposting: a severe hypo (unconscious, fitting, unable to swallow) is a medical emergency needing a 999 call, and nothing should be given by mouth to an unconscious person. The insulin medicine page carries the 999 advice; the class page does not.
findings.suggestedFix: Add: 'Severe hypoglycaemia is an emergency: call 999; nothing is given by mouth to someone who is unconscious.'

findings.quote: Tissues with naturally low metabolic activity, such as the liver and prostate, give little contrast and limit FDG's usefulness there
findings.explanation: The liver is metabolically very active and shows moderate physiological FDG uptake; FDG performs poorly there because of high background uptake and hepatic glucose-6-phosphatase, which removes the phosphate so tracer is not trapped (the site's FDG page lists the liver as that exception). In the prostate the limits are the low glycolytic rate of many prostate cancers and urinary activity in the adjacent bladder. 'Naturally low metabolic activity' is wrong for the liver.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace with 'Some tumours (for example many prostate cancers and some liver tumours) take up little FDG, and physiological uptake or urinary activity near the liver and bladder can obscure disease', or delete the sentence.

findings.quote: Severe skin reactions are more common in children, in people who reacted to an epilepsy medicine, in those allergic to trimethoprim and in those taking sodium valproate
findings.explanation: This is not a recognised risk-factor list for allopurinol (documented risks include HLA-B*58:01, kidney impairment, a high starting dose, the first weeks of treatment, and thiazide/ACE-inhibitor co-prescription, as the page's own interactions say). Children, prior rash on an anticonvulsant and sodium valproate resemble lamotrigine's rash risk factors. It is absent from the allopurinol medicine page and I could not match it to the cited references (NHS allopurinol, FDA Uloric label, NCBI HLA-B*58:01 summary).
findings.suggestedFix: Remove unless it can be matched to the NHS or BNF allopurinol text.

notes: Read all 29 entities in full (both printer ranges). More than 20 candidate issues were found; the 20 above were kept (0 high, 8 medium, 12 low). Lower-priority items not reported as findings: (1) opioids: classWarnings 'Naloxone reverses overdose' has no duration caveat (naloxone is shorter acting than many opioids) or emergency-call advice; the summary calls codeine and tramadol 'strong painkillers' (BNF weak/moderate opioids); no mention of MHRA codeine restrictions (under 12s, breastfeeding, ultra-rapid metabolisers). (2) anticoagulants classInteractions[1] says antiplatelets and SSRIs are 'used only under specialist direction', whereas the SSRI page says 'gastroprotection considered' (SSRI plus anticoagulant is routine with caution). (3) beta-blockers: 'ending in -olol' excludes carvedilol and labetalol (suffix is -lol); the mechanism says propranolol blunts 'sweating', but sweating is cholinergically mediated and is the hypo warning sign beta blockers usually do not mask; 'tiredness is the commonest reason for switching' is unsupported. (4) corticosteroids: 'a proton pump inhibitor for long courses' is a blanket statement (gastroprotection is for those with extra GI risk) and is not on the prednisolone page. (5) macrolides: erythromycin is a moderate, clarithromycin a strong, CYP3A4 inhibitor; 'simvastatin contraindicated with clarithromycin and paused during erythromycin' treats two macrolides the UK SmPC contraindicates alike differently; roxithromycin is not marketed in the UK. (6) NSAIDs: no mention of MHRA cardiovascular contraindications for diclofenac and coxibs; pregnancy wording ('late pregnancy', 'third trimester') may lag current 20-week advice. (7) statins: 'Unexplained muscle pain with dark urine needs a same-day creatine kinase test' (also on the atorvastatin page) is a specific urgency the cited NHS/NICE pages are unlikely to state; 'urgent medical assessment' would be safer. (8) biguanides: 'withheld around contrast' is stated generally, whereas the iodinated-contrast medicine page limits it to reduced kidney function; summary 'without causing hypoglycaemia' is unqualified (not true alongside insulin or sulfonylureas). (9) androgens: check that a testosterone patch ('gel or patch') is currently marketed in the UK. (10) Reference hygiene: vaccines-influenza cites the GOV.UK 2023-to-2024 programme document (superseded; title omits the season); antiplatelets 'NHS: Low-dose aspirin' points at /medicines/aspirin/ (I recall the low-dose page slug is low-dose-aspirin; please check); insulins 'BNF: Insulin' titles point at insulin-aspart URLs; ssris 'NHS: SSRIs' points at the general antidepressants page; stray query strings in the loop-diuretics PMC URL (?utm.com=) and ssris StatPearls URL (?report=printable); NHS patient-information pages are typed 'regulatory'; gadolinium and febuxostat passages cite the FDA only although the site is UK-first (EMA/MHRA positions differ). (11) Root cause of several findings (CCB, beta-blockers, bisphosphonates, statins): class-wide sentences sourced to a single member monograph (amlodipine, bisoprolol, alendronic acid, atorvastatin/ibuprofen). Several aliases are broader than the class (antidepressants for SSRIs, beta-lactam for penicillins, reliever inhalers for bronchodilators). Several class findings (thiazide-like wording, levothyroxine/PPI spacing, rosuvastatin 40 mg) also appear on member medicine pages and should be fixed together. Entities with note-level items only and no reported finding: opioids, antiplatelets, corticosteroids, macrolides, vaccines-influenza, biguanides, androgens, contrast-agents.
